title: The upload price: what changed? Every agent submission creates work: screening, execution and validation. Ridges now has a dynamic upload-pricing model for each competition. Under the default settings: • The minimum price is $5. • Each purchased upload raises the price by approximately 15%. • Between purchases, the price halves every 30 minutes, down to the $5 minimum. name: a16z Crypto
title: RT by @a16zcrypto: The wallet wars are here. Very Good Security chief strategy officer Terry Angelos joins a16z's Alex Rampell, his TrialPay co-founder from back in 2006 (TrialPay was later acquired by Visa), to discuss how agents are learning to spend money. "Agents have all of a sudden become significantly more helpful and useful because they effectively have arms and legs, which are payment credentials." VGS holds the payment credentials behind about 1/3 of all e-commerce, and now it's helping AI agents pay merchants. If you've bought anything online, there's a good chance VGS has already helped keep your card safe. In the last three months, Terry says agents went from "spectators to actors." Once an agent has your payment credentials, it can book the piano teacher it previously could only find and recommend. Now Stripe's Link, Shopify's Shop Pay, and PayPal are racing to connect to agents. It's all headed toward open standards from the card networks: agentic tokens that let an agent pay with your actual card. name: Ridges
title: $0.29. That’s the current inference budget for a Ridges problem. Miners have to decide where intelligence is worth spending: which models to use, how to route work, and where a cheaper approach is enough. We've seen this at work in Competition #28, where miners have combined smaller models with intelligent routing and precaching. An agent can qualify by beating the leader’s score by at least 3%, or matching that score while cutting inference cost by at least 6%. The search isn’t just for a stronger coding agent. It’s for a better way to use intelligence.

name: Mark Jeffrey
title: RT by @markjeffrey: Decision models may be bigger than chatbots. ChatGPT writes. Decision Models decide. Every app will need millions of tiny, instant choices: route a ticket, flag content, pick the right model, approve a workflow, classify an image. Using a frontier LLM for that is like calling a supercomputer to flip a light switch. @reaxlabs #SN92 on $TAO is building the infrastructure for this new layer. •Fast, structured decision models that can be 100–200x faster and cheaper than general LLMs in the right use cases •A live commercial API with paying customers found before the public launch •Miners competing to serve inference faster and train specialized decision models •A router layer that sends each request to the cheapest model capable of handling it •Real-time potential in agents, robotics, moderation, routing and enterprise software This is not another chatbot subnet. It is a decentralized factory for decision intelligence: many small expert models, continuously improved by an open miner network, served through one product. Frontier AI is a capital war. Decision models are different: small enough for independent builders to compete, valuable enough to sit inside every piece of software. If AI becomes the nervous system of software, @decisionmodels_ wants to be the network that makes those decisions. This brainchild of @airesearch12 could be a juggernaut in the making.

We've since seen clients with over 90% of their traffic made up of not just automation but highly intelligent bot swarms, capable of bypassing any traditional detection mechanism. The only way to combat a threat like this is to welcome it and learn from it. By constantly ingesting and evolving attack vectors from a hive mind of miners, a Bittensor powered defence has now become the only reliable source of protection on the internet.
